title: PBOs and metric hypotheses
objective: Write one complete metric hypothesis using What/How/Why.
clearance: Rewritten draft; pending SME and partner clearance

blocks.x: Positive Business Outcomes (PBOs) translate strategy into results a business owner would recognize. Metrics make them measurable. In preparation, both are hypotheses.
From priority to outcome to metric

For each relevant line of business, draft one or two PBOs and three to five candidate metrics. Glean's Metrics Library groups metrics by function and warns against using the same metrics for every persona. A CIO cares about different measures than a sales director.
For each metric, write down three things:

items: **What** is measured: a precise definition, such as "mean handle time for password and access cases."
**How** it will be measured: the system, the time window, and who supplies the data.
**Why** it connects to the outcome: the logic linking the metric to the PBO.

blocks.x: Choose a small, balanced set. A speed metric needs a quality guardrail, so that "faster" doesn't turn into "faster but worse." For support, a balanced set might pair handle time with resolution rate, escalation rate, and cost per resolved case.

blocks.x: These are hypotheses until the metric owners confirm definitions, baselines, and feasibility. Never borrow an industry benchmark and label it the customer's current state.

Glean's value-selling training highlights the question that often matters most: "What are you tracking today?" Metrics the customer already measures are easier to baseline and more credible to finance. If a strong champion already has an analysis for their team, build on it rather than starting from scratch.
